implementation_notes: C's mud form is a small number of .c files that declare most of the system's state as `extern`, so the include graph stops carrying information and the link order decides which definition wins. Diagnosis is cheap and mechanical: `nm` on the object files, or the compiler's own report of every translation unit that touches a given symbol, tells you which modules share which knowledge. Consolidation means moving the state into a struct with accessor functions and making the owning .c file the only definition; that is the only encapsulation C offers, and it is enough. Reconstruction behind a facade is a set of static inline wrappers in a header so callers do not have to change at the same time as the internals.
idiom_name: one translation unit of globals, plus headers included everywhere
pitfalls: `extern "C"` headers spread the global surface across language boundaries, making the dependency graph invisible to per-language tooling.
Static libraries resolve duplicate symbols by link order rather than by error, so conflicting definitions of the same global can survive to runtime.
The `#define`d macro in a shared header is the most entrenched form: it cannot be given an accessor without changing every caller.
